title: UK Diaspora Protests Outside Indian High Commission in London Over Electoral Roll Revision
excerpt: Diaspora groups held an 'Emergency Protest' in London on Tuesday evening in solidarity with demonstrations in New Delhi, backing demands to scrap the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and remove Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
body:
• Diaspora groups protested on Tuesday evening outside the High Commission of India in London over India's electoral roll revision, India Today reported.
  • The "Emergency Protest" was convened by the South Asia Solidarity Group, Cambridge South Asian Forum Against Hindutva, Indian Workers' Association and SOAS Ambedkar Society, among other organisations, with a large number of students attending.
  • Protesters backed two principal demands: removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and scrapping of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
  • No response to the London protest from the High Commission or the Election Commission was reported; the Commission's stated position is that the revision is intended to ensure the accuracy and transparency of the rolls.

Diaspora groups in the United Kingdom protested on Tuesday evening outside the High Commission of India in London over India's electoral roll revision, in solidarity with demonstrations in New Delhi over electoral reforms and the right to protest, India Today reported.

The gathering, described by its organisers as an "Emergency Protest," was convened by the South Asia Solidarity Group, the Cambridge South Asian Forum Against Hindutva, the Indian Workers' Association and the SOAS Ambedkar Society, among other organisations. A large number of students attended, according to the report, which did not give a specific crowd count.

The demands

Protesters backed the demands of student groups and opposition parties in India, principally two: the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and the scrapping of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls — the Election Commission's intensive revision exercise that opposition parties have contested as exclusionary, and that has become the central flashpoint of India's current electoral-reform fight.

https://x.com/NewIndianXpress/status/2110290853323493539

The other side

No response from the High Commission, the Chief Election Commissioner or the Election Commission specifically to the London protest was reported. The Commission's previously stated position, as framed in the report's background, is that the revision is intended to ensure the accuracy and transparency of the electoral rolls. In India, the SIR dispute has pitted the Commission against opposition parties and student groups demanding the exercise be halted — the same demands the London protesters carried.

Why a London protest matters

Protests outside the High Commission are a recurring feature of diaspora politics, but they are also a transmission mechanism: disputes over voting rights in India resonate directly with overseas Indians, many of whom remain Indian citizens and voters, or have family members whose names sit on the rolls being revised. The organiser list — student societies, workers' associations and South Asia solidarity groups rather than a single community body — reflects how the SIR fight is being framed in the diaspora: as an electoral-rights issue, not a partisan one.

What to watch

Whether the London action is repeated or spreads to other diaspora hubs, and whether the Election Commission addresses the overseas protests directly. In India, the next developments are in the SIR timeline itself and in the political and legal challenges to it in New Delhi.
